newsitem.title: UK: Who might be who in UK Labour cabinet.
newsitem.headline: Who might be who in UK Labour cabinet.

text.p: The celebrations if Labour win Britain's election on Thursday will not last long before party leader Tony Blair suffers his first headaches of government.
His first problem if he becomes prime minister will be who to include in Britain's first Labour cabinet for 18 years.
It is a problem posed by a clash between Labour party rules and British law. Party rules mean Blair should include all those now in the opposition "shadow cabinet" -- a total of 19.
But that is without Blair and his deputy, John Prescott.

A cabinet also needs a leader of the House of Lords and a Lord Chancellor -- a legal post tipped to go to Derry (now Lord) Irvine, the lawyer who took Blair and his wife, Cherie Booth, on as trainee lawyers 21 years ago.

Add at least four key members of Blair's team -- five with campaign supremo Peter Mandelson -- who were not voted on to the shadow cabinet, where the result often reflects internal party politics rather than ability, and the list hits 27 or 28.
In the House of Commons, Blair has a legal limit of 95 ministerial posts, including party managers or whips, with 15 more in the upper House of Lords.
But the cabinet is limited by law to 22 paid posts. The result is likely to be a few frustrated would-be ministers who could end up causing Blair problems in the long term.
Key names are already certain -- although last minute surprises cannot be ruled out.

Economics spokesman Gordon Brown, whose decision not to contest the Labour leadership contest in 1994 virtually handed victory to Tony Blair, is certain to be confirmed as Chancellor of the Exchequer.
Foreign affairs spokesman Robin Cook looks sure to take over the Foreign Office, although his preference would be a return to his old trade and industry portfolio or even to supplant Brown.

Blair's deputy leader John Prescott poses more of a problem. He has been promised a "big job" in government as a reward for his loyalty and his work to keep traditional supporters on board during Blair's radical overhaul of the party.
But exactly what constitutes a "big job" is not clear, although he could become deputy prime minister.

Education spokesman David Blunkett has been guaranteed a role in education, but home affairs spokesman Jack Straw will be anxiously awaiting his confirmation as Home Secretary after some poor parliamentary performances against incumbent Conservative Michael Howard.

Social Security spokeswoman Harriet Harman is also tipped for the cabinet. Despite angering rank and file Labour party members by sending her son to a selective school in defiance of party policy, she is a member of Blair's inner circle.

Labour's health spokesman, Chris Smith, the only member of parliament to have declared his homosexuality openly, is also tipped for a cabinet role. So, too, is trade and industry spokeswoman Margaret Beckett, who briefly became Labour's first woman leader when she stepped in as caretaker after John Smith's death in 1994 and who topped the latest shadow election poll.

Scottish spokesman George Robertson is also well-placed, and Northern Ireland spokeswoman Marjorie Mowlam is almost certain to retain her job, particularly after her public image was boosted by a recent battle to recover from a brain tumour.
Another certainty is public services minister Derek Foster, who was publicly promised a cabinet job in return for stepping down as chief whip, although his cabinet role is far from clear.
But that leaves just seven posts, one of which must go to the leader of the House of Lords, as well as the controversial figure of Mandelson, the man in charge of campaign planning.
Mandelson is admired and loathed in equal measure by Conservatives -- who see him as the brain behind Labour's campaign -- and many Labour MPs -- who resent his influence.
Mandelson may miss the cabinet this time. But not for long.
